crosby_ecological.title: Alfred W. Crosby, Ecological Imperialism: The Biological Expansion of Europe, 900–1900 (1986; second edition 2004).
crosby_ecological.citation: Alfred W. Crosby, Ecological Imperialism: The Biological Expansion of Europe, 900–1900 (1986; second edition 2004).

verification.note: Publisher description consulted for the argument about organisms and European settlement in temperate regions. Original 1986 metadata checked in the indexed Folger catalogue https://catalog.folger.edu/record/47488 ; direct catalogue access failed and publisher front-matter download timed out. This is the book’s stated argument, not a full reading or an endorsement of biological reductionism. Addendum 2026-10-13: Cambridge University Press sample PDFs of the second edition (assets.cambridge.org, ISBN 9780521546188: front matter, 18 pp.; excerpt, 10 pp.; image-only, OCR'd) read: imprint ('First published 1986; Canto edition first published 1993; Second edition first published 2004'), contents pp. xi–xii, 2004 preface pp. xv–xx, acknowledgments pp. xxi–xxii, prologue pp. 1–7 and the opening of chapter 2, pp. 8–10. Page numbers are the 2004 edition's; the 1986 edition (Open Library OL2713233M: xiv, 368 p., [16] p. of plates, ISBN 0521320097) has the same length as the 2004 body plus index, but its pagination was not seen. Quoted: 'European emigrants and their descendants are all over the place, which requires explanation'; 'Europeans, in contrast, seem to have leapfrogged around the globe'; 'what I shall call the Neo-Europes, lands thousands of kilometers from Europe and from each other' (p. 2); 'factors perhaps best described as biogeographical' (p. 5); 'European flora and fauna, including human beings, can thrive in these regions if the competition is not too fierce'; 'what in heaven's name is the reason that the sun never sets on the empire of the dandelion? Perhaps the success of European imperialism has a biological, an ecological, component' (p. 7). Contents: 'The Norse and the Crusaders' (41), 'The Fortunate Isles' (70), 'Winds' (104), 'Weeds' (145), 'Animals' (171), 'Ills' (195), 'New Zealand' (217), 'Explanations' (269), 'Conclusion' (294). Acknowledgments: 'William McNeill, who read the whole thing in first draft' (p. xxii); parts first appeared in Environmental Review and The Texas Quarterly. The 2004 preface (later) calls Pomeranz's The Great Divergence 'The clearest exposition of the new scenario' (p. xvii, n.) and says 'I am proud to have contributed to it' (p. xx). Chapters 2–12 are unread.

pe131_cronon_uses_1993.title: William Cronon, “The Uses of Environmental History,” Environmental History Review 17, no. 3 (Fall 1993): 1–22.
pe131_cronon_uses_1993.citation: William Cronon, “The Uses of Environmental History” (ASEH presidential address), Environmental History Review 17:3 (1993): 1–22. doi:10.2307/3984602.

verification.note: Author-hosted scan (no text layer) OCR’d locally at 300 dpi; page numbers from the running heads (two pages per image); Crossref 10.2307/3984602 agrees. OCR letter errors corrected only where unambiguous; the p. 8 passage was checked against the page image ('one of a favorite metaphor' is as printed). Read: pp. 1–9, 12–20 and notes pp. 20–22; pp. 10–11 not read closely. Passages used: the new histories 'born or reenergized in the wake of the 1960s' and the interventionist practitioners Nash, Hays, Worster, Merchant, Tarr and Pyne (pp. 2–3, nn. 2–7); 'nature' as 'a fundamental category of historical analysis' (p. 4); the market lesson, 'a central concern of my own work' (p. 8, n. 14); lessons footnoted to Crosby, White, Merchant, McEvoy, Melosi (pp. 8–10, nn. 15–25); 'All human history has a natural context' and 'One important contribution of environmental history' (p. 13); kinship with 'a Braudelian vision of history' (p. 14); 'All environmental knowledge is culturally constructed and historically contingent—including our own' (p. 14) and the realist pairing (p. 15); history as 'parables, not policy recommendations or certainties' (p. 16); the chief moral of Changes in the Land, Leopold’s tree rings and 'material history … spiritual history … political economic history' (p. 19). canon-evidence-international.md (text A) records an independent OCR reading of the same scan. [Also checked under pe131_crosby_cronon_1993: Author-hosted scan, OCR'd for the canon evidence file on 2026-10-13; pp. 8 and 10 and notes 16 and 25 (p. 22) re-read, with page assignment checked against the running heads of the page images. Crossref 10.2307/3984602: Environmental History Review 17(3), September 1993, 1–22 (Cronon's ASEH presidential address). Lessons of the field: 'When people migrate from one ecosystem to another, they carry with them other organisms—plants, animals, microbes—whose success or failure in the new location is often crucial in determining the success or failure of the migration' (p. 8, n. 16); 'Beware of bugs that come from afar' (p. 10, n. 25). Note 16 cites The Columbian Exchange (1972) and Ecological Imperialism (1986); note 25 cites both again. Other drafts in this batch may cite the same address under their own ids; merge at build if so.] [Also checked under pe131_leopold_cronon_1993: Scanned PDF from the author's site, read in full through OCR (pp. 1–22, notes included); superscript note numbers are not reliably readable in the OCR. p. 19: 'Environmental history tries to reconstruct the endless layers of change that we and the earth have traced upon each other. It is the history recorded in Aldo Leopold’s tree rings, the history recorded by the marks of his saw upon the good oak as he cut it down, the history recorded by the memories in the hatted head with its shadow on the stump'; n. 32 (p. 22): 'The echo here is that of Leopold’s “Good Oak,” Sand County Almanac, 6-18.' n. 11 (p. 21): 'At this and several other points in this essay, I trust that readers will hear my echoes of Aldo Leopold's Sand County Almanac (New York: Oxford University Press, 1949), 224-25.' By note order, n. 11 falls on p. 7, where some environmental historians measure 'usefulness' 'by whether or not it contributes to the health and integrity of natural systems'. It places the field's origins in 'the political movement that helped spawn it' (p. 2).] [Also checked under pe131_merchant_cronon_1993: Author-hosted scan OCR'd; pp. 2–3, 8–9 and notes 5, 13 and 18 read for Merchant. 'Carolyn Merchant joined Worster in bringing an environmentalist perspective to the history of science, but combined it with a more feminist approach to argue in The Death of Nature that western science has harmed nature and women in parallel ways; her Radical Ecology, though less historical, is still more activist in its efforts to intervene in contemporary political struggles' (p. 3; n. 5). Lesson footnoted to Death of Nature and Ecological Revolutions (n. 18): 'Men and women often experience the world in very different ways, so that one cannot hope to understand the way a culture relates to an environment without examining the ways it engenders the natural world' (p. 9). Other agents drafting 1.131 entries may cite the same essay under another id; merge at release.] [Also checked under pe131_richard_white_cronon_1993: Author's scanned PDF, OCR'd for canon-evidence-international.md (2026-10-13); the White passages were re-read in that OCR. Among his 'lessons' (pp. 8–9): 'In American history, the horse was not simply a European invader, but a complex cultural entity that became attached to different human communities in very different ways' (p. 9), with n. 23 'White, Roots of Dependency'; n. 15 cites White, Land Use, Environment, and Social Change (1980) and The Roots of Dependency with Calvin Martin. Page attributions follow the canon file's reading of the running heads.] [Also checked under pe131_extras_cronon_uses_1993: Author-hosted scan re-downloaded and OCR'd for this draft (OCR letter errors corrected only where unambiguous). Read pp. 1–3, 8–9, 14–15 and notes pp. 20–22. Quoted: Nash's Wilderness and the American Mind 'has played a significant role in helping frame debates about wilderness protection' (pp. 2–3); Hays's Conservation and the Gospel of Efficiency and Beauty, Health, and Permanence 'speak just as powerfully to major trends in conservation and environmental politics in the twentieth century' (p. 3); 'Steven [sic] Pyne's epic histories of fire have consistently tried to persuade present-day resource managers of the complexity of their task' (p. 3); n. 6 (p. 21): 'Pyne's classic work in American history is Stephen J. Pyne, Fire in America'; lessons: fire (pp. 8–9, n. 17 Pyne) and 'Early conservationists were obsessed with questions of economically efficient production, while later environmentalists have been equally obsessed with questions of ecologically responsible consumption' (p. 9, n. 20 Hays); 'some kinship with a Braudelian vision of history' (p. 14, n. 29 The Mediterranean); n. 27 (p. 22): 'Nash's whig history of wilderness consciousness and the rights of nature'.]

pe131_worster_jah_1990.title: Donald Worster, “Transformations of the Earth: Toward an Agroecological Perspective in History,” Journal of American History 76, no. 4 (March 1990): 1087–1106.
pe131_worster_jah_1990.citation: Donald Worster, “Transformations of the Earth: Toward an Agroecological Perspective in History,” Journal of American History 76:4 (1990): 1087–1106, opening “A Round Table: Environmental History”. doi:10.2307/2936586.

verification.note: English JAH text unread: the DOI resolves to the OUP page, which returned 403, and JSTOR returned a bot challenge. Crossref 10.2307/2936586 gives JAH 76:4, first page 1087; Crossref lists the round table's responses: Crosby 'An Enthusiastic Second' (1107), White 'Environmental History, Ecology, and Meaning' (1111), Merchant 'Gender and Environmental History' (1117), Cronon 'Modes of Prophecy and Production' (1122), Pyne 'Firestick History' (1132) and Worster's reply 'Seeing Beyond Culture' (1142). The whole article and notes were read in Portuguese translation ('Transformações da terra', Ambiente & Sociedade 5:2/6:1, 2002–03, pp. 23–44). The English wording quoted in this packet comes from Worster's reprint of the essay in The Wealth of Nature (1993, ch. 4; see pe131_worster_wealth_1993), checked by full-text search. JAH pages are given only where Isenberg 2013 cites them: p. 1091 for 'at once materialist and idealist' and 'the analysis of modes of production as ecological phenomena', both matching the 1993 wording. Worster's reply and the White, Cronon, Crosby and Pyne responses are unread. [Also checked under pe131_leopold_worster_1990: The English original was not seen (JSTOR blocked; no open copy found). Crossref 10.2307/2936586 confirms JAH 76:4 (March 1990), first page 1087. The Portuguese translation was read in the PDF of orgprints eprint 20347 (Worster_transformações.pdf), whose first-page note says the article was first published in the Journal of American History in March 1990. Quoted from the translation: p. 23, 'Há quarenta anos atrás, um homem sábio e visionário, o conservacionista e biólogo da vida selvagem, Aldo Leopold, de Wisconsin, reivindicou uma “interpretação ecológica da História”, pela qual propunha usar as idéias e a pesquisa do emergente campo da ecologia para ajudar a explicar porque os fatos que constituem o passado desenvolveram-se da maneira como os conhecemos'; 'Levou algum tempo para os historiadores darem atenção ao conselho de Leopold, mas finalmente o campo da história ambiental começou a ganhar forma e seus praticantes estão tentando construir a partir de sua iniciativa.' p. 24: 'os fatos no caso são mais complicados do que Leopold poderia ter explorado nos limites de seu ensaio, e eles exigem mais do que uma forma simples de determinismo ambiental, que é o que um leitor menos atento poderia encontrar em seu exemplo'; Kentucky bluegrass 'não era uma espécie nativa, mas uma importação européia', followed by Crosby's 'imperialismo ecológico'. Notes, p. 42: n. 1 cites Leopold, A Sand County Almanac, and Sketches Here and There (1949; reprinted New York, 1987), p. 205; n. 3 says Leopold knew the story was more complex and quotes him (p. 206) that 'we do not even know' where bluegrass came from. English glosses in the atlas are the editor's, not Worster's words. A Bowdoin course guide paraphrasing the essay was seen and not used.] [Also checked under pe131_richard_white_worster_1990: Only the Portuguese translation was read (orgprints eprint 20347 PDF). Note 5 (translation p. 42): 'O melhor esforço para traçar a emergência do campo, pelo menos em uma parte influente do mundo, é o de WHITE, R. “American Environmental History: The Development of a New Historical Field” … White argumenta que o estudo da fronteira e da história do oeste tem sido a influência formativa neste campo. Uma outra fonte de idéias importante, realmente retirada da influência de Frederick Jackson Turner, tem sido a dos historiadores e geógrafos franceses, particularmente Fernand Braudel, Lucien Febvre e Emmanuel Le Roy Ladurie, todos associados à revista dos Annales.' The English wording and JAH page of the note are unchecked.] Addendum 2026-10-13: Re-read for edge_111 (extras packet): note 5 in the Portuguese translation (Ambiente & Sociedade 5:2/6:1, 2002–03, p. 42, n. 5), from the orgprints PDF, names 'Fernand Braudel, Lucien Febvre e Emmanuel Le Roy Ladurie, todos associados à revista dos Annales' as 'Uma outra fonte de idéias importante'. It is attached to the sentence that introduces the new field of ecological or environmental history. The English JAH page remains unread.
